newsitem.title: BELGIUM: FOCUS - EU probes firms over Cuba issue.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - EU probes firms over Cuba issue.

text.p: The European Commission is investigating dozens of companies it believes are breaking EU laws and undermining efforts to counter Washington's Helms-Burton Act, trade sources have told Reuters.

Commission officials admitted on Tuesday they were attempting to get more information from European companies on their Cuban links and would like to see more cooperation from companies which are affected by the act.

"The anti-blocking legislation is a powerful response to Helms-Burton," said Peter Guilford, spokesman for Trade Commissioner Sir Leon Brittan. "Inevitably it puts companies in a difficult position ... to make it effective we have to dig."
The EU's blocking laws were passed in October as a foil to part of the Helms-Burton Act, the culmination of years of U.S. policy aimed at isolating the Cuban government of Fidel Castro.

Among other things, the U.S. act allows naturalised Americans to sue any foreign company or individual deemed to have gained from investments in property confiscated by the Cuban government since the communist revolution of 1959.

Although this section has twice been suspended by President Bill Clinton, the U.S. state department has pressed ahead with compiling a watch list against foreign companies which may be investing in such property.

To counter this, the EU passed tit-for-tat laws making it illegal for European companies to cooperate with U.S. investigations and also to prevent firms from pulling out of Cuba on the basis of a U.S. probe.
The blocking laws were designed to present a unified European response to the U.S. act -- which the EU considers extra-territorial -- and also to protect companies which choose not to disinvest.
But trade sources said the Commission has not received a single response to calls for European companies to identify themselves if the U.S. State Department contacted them.
"The Commission is very, very disappointed with the lack of support it is getting ... and has started to take action," one trade analyst told Reuters.

"They are keeping it quiet, but the European Commission is looking into the activities of dozens of companies to see if they have broken the law," he said. Sources would not say which companies were being investigated.
Although Washington will not say how many or which companies it has identified, trade analysts say it is "a great deal more" than the three identified last year.

Executives from Italian telecoms company Stet, Canadian mining conglomorate Sherrit International and Mexican telecoms firm Grupo Domo were placed on a U.S. blacklist in July and barred from entering the U.S. because of their links to Cuba.

"By not coming forward, the Commission believes these companies are playing right into the hands of the Americans," a trade expert said. "The Commission believes this undermines its action in trying to overturn the Act."
Under the EU's blocking laws, companies are obliged to tell the Commission as soon as they are approached.
It is up to individual members states, however, to ensure companies abide by the law and to prosecute firms in breach.
Guilford said he believed some companies might not be aware of the full implications of the blocking laws or that they could apply for a waiver.
Under the EU's laws, companies with substantial interests in the U.S. as well as Cuba can apply for a waiver if their assets are threatened.
